title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Personal and fitness training
audience: Personal trainers who need a base hourly rate, a package rate and a minimum charge before they quote, including solo trainers
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the trainer's own costs and income target, then compare it with public local evidence.
Set a minimum charge for short visits and explain it to a client before the session.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A personal trainer's rate depends on experience, the specialist skills offered, how scarce those skills are locally, the range of work offered and the cost of running the business. A trainer who offers one-to-one sessions, small groups and workplace programmes can justify a higher rate, because a client can book several needs with one provider. Local price evidence should come from public price lists you can check. City of Sydney Leisure's council list shows a single 30-minute session at $71 and a single 60-minute session at $112.60 (fetched 9 November 2026). Its fortnightly direct debit for one 60-minute session a week is $201.40, which is $100.70 a session. Those are one council's prices with its own cost base. Competitor evidence should come from insured, qualified practitioners, not from a single published average.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Trainers often price as though every hour of the week can be billed. Few can. Travel between clients, gaps between sessions, programme planning, progress notes, marketing, professional development and insurance admin are not billable, and neither are cancellations and leave. Jobber says billable time typically makes up 60 to 80 per cent of working hours (Jobber, published 5 November 2024, modified 20 July 2026). That is a general range, not a fitness figure, so check your own log against it. Rebate-eligible trainers also need 20 CPD hours a year (AUSactive, modified 23 June 2026), and that time is non-billable. For example, if 60 of every 100 paid hours are billable, the costs of all 100 hours must come out of the 60, so the rate is about 1.67 times the rate for a fully billable week.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, such as insurance, equipment and its upkeep, booking software, marketing, accounting, CPR and first aid, and the vehicle and phone, to the income you need. Divide the total by billable hours to reach the base rate. The AIPT personal training guide works backwards from a target income: divide the income by working weeks, then by weekly hours, and add tax and business costs on top. Its example is $90,000 across 46 weeks at 30 hours, which gives about $65 an hour before tax and expenses (AIPT, 16 May 2025). That is a worked model, not a market rate. If you employ trainers, on-costs apply. A Jobber cleaning guide says payroll tax, workers' compensation, training and unpaid travel can add 25 to 40 per cent on top of wages, and that cleaners often undercount them (Jobber, 31 March 2026). That is a cleaning source, so check the figures for personal training. Have a registered tax agent confirm how leave and superannuation apply to your situation before the rate is published.

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short visits
instruction.body: A short session still needs travel to a client's site, set-up and admin. The shorter the session, the less its price covers those fixed minutes. The council's prices show that a short session is not simply half the price of a long one: a 30-minute single is $71 and a 60-minute single is $112.60 (City of Sydney Leisure). A minimum charge might apply to home or site visits, trial sessions or short check-ins. One contractor pricing guide suggests setting the minimum from the full cost of the visit, dividing that cost by one minus the target margin, with the minimum covering travel, set-up and clean-up (Contractor+, 23 September 2026). That guide labels its figures illustrative, so this lesson uses the method only. State the minimum before the visit, in writing, and explain what it covers.

instruction.heading: Reviewing the rate and comparing with others
instruction.body: Business Victoria recommends reviewing prices about every three months, to check that they still suit the business and its customers (Business Victoria, no date shown). Xero recommends reviewing prices at least once a year (Xero Australia, 3 September 2026). Competitor prices are a guide, not a target, and Business Victoria warns not to assume a rival's prices are right. Compare only with insured, qualified practitioners, because credentials, clients and costs differ. Honour packages already sold at the old rate, and give clients notice before a new rate applies.

procedure: Log paid and billable hours for one month, then estimate the year's billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, equipment, booking software, marketing, accounting, CPR and first aid, CPD and vehicle.
Add the income needed, including leave and tax allowances confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin for a short visit, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only, not market rates. A trainer's log shows 30 paid hours a week, of which 22 are billable (illustrative). She plans to set the rate as though all 30 hours could be billed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What does the wrong assumption do to the rate, and what should she do instead?
workedExamples.reasoning: Pricing as if every paid hour were billable understates the rate, because the costs and income still have to come out of the hours that can be billed. A rate built on 30 hours would be about 27 per cent below a rate built on 22 hours (22 divided by 30 is about 0.73). She should build the rate from the 22 billable hours, using her costs and income target, then check it against public price lists from insured practitioners and against her minimum charge before she publishes it.

equipmentAndPpe: Log of paid and billable hours for one month
Price sheet with the base rate, the package rate and the minimum charge

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a published average or a competitor's figure without checking the costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from the trainer's own costs and billable hours, then compare it with public local evidence.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking short visits at the same rate, without covering travel and set-up.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law, as summarised in the ACCC's guidance on setting prices. That guidance does not cover minimum or call-out charges, or what counts as a fair term. Check those points against current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet.
Tax and superannuation for employed trainers and for the owner: confirm with a registered tax agent. This lesson does not state tax treatment.
Health screening: not verified. No screening standard for personal training was found in the research, so none is set out here. Check your insurer's and professional body's requirements.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the trainer's costs and income target, and is compared with public local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short visit.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the package rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against public local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for short visits.

knowledgeChecks.question: An owner can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and so the client pays less per job
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average published on a website and from the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay and the owner's own mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for short jobs?
options: Because short jobs need travel but no setup time at all and the admin takes no time
Because travel, setup and admin time does not shrink with the size of the job
Because clients expect every job to cost the same amount, whatever its size
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every job the owner takes

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate?
options: A single published national average from the largest trade body
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as super, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure.

Jobber, 'What are billable hours', https://getjobber.com/academy/what-are-billable-hours/, published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026. Supports: billable time at about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours; a general range, not an Australian figure.

AIPT, 'Personal Training Prices: Setting the Right Rates', https://www.aipt.edu.au/articles/personal-training-prices-how-much-should-you-charge, 16 May 2025. Supports: working backwards from a target income. Example figures are a model, not a market rate.

Jobber, 'How Much to Charge for House Cleaning', https://getjobber.com/academy/cleaning/how-much-to-charge-for-house-cleaning/, 31 March 2026. Cleaning source, not fitness. Supports: on-costs of 25 to 40 per cent that owners tend to undercount.

Contractor+, 'Minimum Service Call Charge: A Contractor's Pricing Guide', https://contractorplus.app/blog/minimum-service-call-charge, 23 September 2026. Supports the method only; the source labels its figures illustrative.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Supports: review prices about every three months; do not assume rivals' prices are right.
Xero Australia, 'How to price services', https://www.xero.com/au/guides/how-to-price-services/, dated 3 September 2026. Supports: review prices at least once a year.

AUSactive, 'Private health fund rebates for personal trainers', https://ausactive.org.au/private-health-fund-rebates-for-personal-trainers/, modified 23 June 2026. Supports: 20 CPD hours a year for rebate-eligible trainers.

City of Sydney Leisure, 'Personal training', https://cityofsydneyleisure.com.au/health-and-wellbeing/personal-training, page date not shown, fetched 9 November 2026. One council's public prices; not a market rate.
